Lab 1: Introduction to R and the {tidyverse}

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 1

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

Welcome to the first lab of Intermediate Quantitative Methods. The labs run alongside the seminar and have two goals:

  • practice the quantitative tools from each week’s seminar, and
  • build your programming skills in R for the rest of your PhD.

This first lab is mostly about the second goal. The syllabus assumes some familiarity with R, but people arrive with very different backgrounds. Some of you have written packages and some have mostly used Stata or SPSS. Today we make sure everyone shares the same toolkit and the same grammar for working with data, which we will use for the rest of the term.

Plan for today ≈ time
Setup: R, the IDE, projects 10 min
R basics: objects, vectors, indexing, functions 25 min
Importing survey data (the European Social Survey) 10 min
Data wrangling with the {tidyverse} 40 min
Functions, iteration, and our first simulation (link to Week 1) 20 min
Wrap-up and best practices 5 min

R, the IDE, and projects 🛠

R and your IDE

R is the language, and the IDE (integrated development environment) is where you write and run it. In this course you can use either:

  • Positron, Posit’s newer IDE, built on VS Code, which works with R and Python, or
  • RStudio, the classic R IDE.

Both have the same four areas:

  1. Console: type code, press <ENTER>, and R runs it. Anything you type here is gone when you close the session.
  2. Script / document editor: where you write code you want to keep, in .R scripts or .qmd Quarto documents like this one.
  3. Environment: the objects you have created. If you run myresult <- 5 + 3 + 2, myresult appears here.
  4. Plots, files, help: graphics output, your file browser, and documentation (try ?mean).

To run a line of code from the editor, place your cursor on it and press Cmd + Enter (macOS) or Ctrl + Enter (Windows/Linux). To run several lines, highlight them first.

print("Hello world!")
[1] "Hello world!"

Projects 🏠

Before you write any code for this course, create a project. A project is a folder that R treats as home. Every path is relative to that folder, so your code runs on your laptop, your co-author’s laptop, and the replication archive of the journal you publish in.

  • RStudio: File > New Project > New Directory. This creates a .Rproj file. Open that file to start working.
  • Positron: File > Open Folder.... The folder is the project.

A good starting structure for this course (and for your dissertation chapters):

.
+-- int-quant-labs.Rproj
+-- data
|   +-- raw          <- never edit these files by hand
|   +-- processed
+-- labs
|   +-- 01-intro-r-tidyverse.qmd
+-- output
|   +-- figures
|   +-- tables
+-- README.md

⚠️ Avoid setwd("/Users/myname/Desktop/..."). Your absolute path only exists on your computer. In a project you can write haven::read_dta("data/ess11_lab.dta") and it works anywhere.

R basics 🧱

R as a calculator

Operator Example
Addition + 2 + 4
Subtraction - 2 - 4
Multiplication * 2 * 4
Division / 4 / 2
Exponentiation ^ 2^4
Square root sqrt() sqrt(144)
Absolute value abs() abs(-4) 
4 * 9
[1] 36
sqrt(144)
[1] 12

Logical operators

Operator
Less than <
Less than or equal to <=
Greater than >
Greater than or equal to >=
Exactly equal to ==
Not equal to !=
Not x !x
x or y x | y
x and y x & y
x in a set y x %in% y

You will use logical operators constantly for data cleaning (keep respondents older than 18), subsetting (only Italy), and recoding (1 if born abroad).

4 > 2
[1] TRUE
4 <= 2
[1] FALSE
"IT" %in% c("DE", "FR", "IT")
[1] TRUE

Objects and assignment

R stores information in objects. We assign values to objects with <-.

  • Names can contain letters, numbers, _, and ., but they cannot start with a number.
  • R is case sensitive: result and Result are different objects.
  • Avoid names that are already functions (mean, sum, data).
  • Anything after # is a comment and is not executed.
result <- 5 / 3
result
[1] 1.666667
result <- 5 - 3 # assigning again overwrites the old value
result
[1] 2

I use <- to assign objects and = to set arguments inside functions, for example mean(x, na.rm = TRUE).

Data types

Type Example Typical use in our data
Numeric 8.5 age, years of education, a 0–10 scale
Integer 8L counts
Character "Italy" country names, open answers
Logical TRUE results of comparisons, dummies
Factor factor("low") categorical variables with fixed levels (e.g., regime type) 
numeric_object <- 8.5
character_object <- "This is a string"
logical_object <- TRUE
factor_object <- factor("Flawed democracy")

class(numeric_object)
[1] "numeric"
class(factor_object)
[1] "factor"

Vectors

A vector is a sequence of elements of the same type. It is the building block of almost everything in R, including the columns of a data frame. We create vectors with c() (combine).

Suppose we have the 2024 population (in millions) of the five most populous countries, from the World Bank:

pop1 <- c(1451, 1409, 340, 283, 251)
country_name <- c("IND", "CHN", "USA", "IDN", "PAK")
asia <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
regime <- factor(c("Flawed democracy", "Autocracy", "Flawed democracy",
                   "Flawed democracy", "Hybrid regime"))

str(pop1)
 num [1:5] 1451 1409 340 283 251
str(regime)
 Factor w/ 3 levels "Autocracy","Flawed democracy",..: 2 1 2 2 3

Activity 💡

Why won’t R let us run either of these?

not_good <- (a, b, c)

not_good_either <- c(one, two, three)

➨ Click for Answer 🔓

The first line is missing the c() function, so R does not know what to do with (a, b, c). The second line has no quotation marks, so R looks for objects called one, two, and three, which do not exist. c("one", "two", "three") would work.

Activity 💡

What is the class of each of these vectors? Why?

mixed_1 <- c(TRUE, "TRUE")
mixed_2 <- c(1, "2", 3)
mixed_3 <- c(1, TRUE, FALSE)
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
class(mixed_1)
[1] "character"
class(mixed_2)
[1] "character"
class(mixed_3)
[1] "numeric"

A vector can only hold one type, so R silently coerces the elements to the most flexible type: logical → numeric → character. This matters when you import survey data: a single "don't know" typed into a numeric column turns the whole column into text.

Vector operations and functions

Arithmetic on vectors is applied element by element:

pop1 * 1e6 # population in persons rather than millions
[1] 1.451e+09 1.409e+09 3.400e+08 2.830e+08 2.510e+08

Functions are reusable pieces of code that take inputs (arguments) and return an output. Some you will use every day:

Function Returns
min(), max() minimum and maximum
sum() the sum
length() the number of elements
mean(), median() mean and median
var(), sd() variance and standard deviation
round(x, digits) x rounded
table() frequency table 
mean(pop1)
[1] 746.8
sd(pop1)
[1] 624.6641
table(regime)
regime
       Autocracy Flawed democracy    Hybrid regime 
               1                3                1

Activity 💡

Without using mean(), how else could we compute the mean population?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
sum(pop1) / length(pop1)
[1] 746.8

Indexing: accessing elements with [ ]

R uses 1-based indexing: the first element is at position 1.

pop1[1] # first element
[1] 1451
pop1[c(2, 5)] # second and fifth elements
[1] 1409  251
pop1[-5] # everything except the fifth element
[1] 1451 1409  340  283
pop1[-length(pop1)] # everything except the last one (more general)
[1] 1451 1409  340  283

We can name the elements of a vector and use a logical condition inside the brackets. Filtering data works exactly like this.

names(pop1) <- country_name
pop1
 IND  CHN  USA  IDN  PAK 
1451 1409  340  283  251 
pop1[names(pop1) == "PAK"]
PAK 
251 
pop1[asia] # only TRUE elements are kept
 IND  CHN  IDN  PAK 
1451 1409  283  251

We can also modify elements. Say we entered Pakistan’s regime type (from the Economist Intelligence Unit) incorrectly:

regime[5] <- "Autocracy" # fix a data entry error
regime
[1] Flawed democracy Autocracy        Flawed democracy Flawed democracy
[5] Autocracy       
Levels: Autocracy Flawed democracy Hybrid regime

Activity 💡

  1. Access all population values greater than or equal to the mean population.
  2. Access all population values smaller than the maximum, but exclude the US.
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
pop1[pop1 >= mean(pop1)]
 IND  CHN 
1451 1409 
pop1[pop1 < max(pop1) & names(pop1) != "USA"]
 CHN  IDN  PAK 
1409  283  251

Missing values: NA

NA is how R denotes missing values. In survey data they are everywhere (refusals, “don’t know”, questions not asked in some countries). Many functions return NA if any value is missing, which is a deliberate choice to make you notice:

trust <- c(4, 1, 2, NA, 3)
mean(trust)
[1] NA
mean(trust, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 2.5
sum(is.na(trust)) # how many are missing?
[1] 1

Other data structures, briefly

  • Lists can hold elements of different types and lengths, even other lists. Regression output in R is stored as a list.
  • Data frames are lists of vectors of equal length: each column is a variable and each row an observation. This is where you will spend most of your time.
my_list <- list(country = "Italy", scores = c(5, 7, 3), eu_member = TRUE)
my_list$scores
[1] 5 7 3
my_df <- data.frame(country = c("Italy", "Hungary", "Sweden"),
                    polyarchy = c(0.86, 0.49, 0.87))
my_df
my_df$polyarchy # the $ operator extracts a column (a vector)
[1] 0.86 0.49 0.87
my_df[2, ] # [row, column]

Packages and importing data 📦

Installing and loading packages

Packages extend R. You install a package once per computer and load it every session.

install.packages("tidyverse") # run once, in the CONSOLE (never inside a .qmd)
library(tidyverse) # run every session, at the top of your script

⚠️ Tip: Do not include install.packages() in your Quarto documents. The document would try to reinstall everything every time you render it.

For today, make sure these are installed:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven"))
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and visualization
library(haven) # import Stata, SPSS, and SAS files

The double colon operator ::

Throughout the labs I write functions as package::function(), for example dplyr::filter(). This:

  • tells you (and your future self) where a function comes from, and
  • avoids conflicts. When you loaded the {tidyverse} above, R warned that dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter(): two packages have a function with the same name, and the last one loaded wins.

Our data: the European Social Survey 🇪🇺

Most of you will work with survey data at some point, and the European Social Survey (ESS) is one of the workhorses of European political science and sociology. We will use a subset of ESS Round 11 (2023/24): about 40,000 respondents in 24 countries.

Variable Description
cntry Country (ISO 2-letter code)
idno Respondent ID
anweight Analysis weight (design × post-stratification × population size)
agea Age
gndr Gender (1 = male, 2 = female)
eduyrs Years of full-time education completed
hinctnta Household income decile (1–10, within country)
domicil Place of residence (big city … farm)
brncntr Born in country (1 = yes, 2 = no)
lrscale Left–right self-placement (0 = left, 10 = right)
polintr Interest in politics (1 = very, 4 = not at all)
vote Voted in the last national election (1 = yes, 2 = no, 3 = not eligible)
stfdem Satisfaction with how democracy works (0–10)
trstplt, trstprl Trust in politicians / parliament (0–10)
imwbcnt Immigrants make country a worse (0) or better (10) place to live
imueclt Country’s cultural life undermined (0) or enriched (10) by immigrants
rlgdgr How religious (0–10)
ppltrst Most people can be trusted (0–10)
happy How happy are you (0–10)

Importing a Stata file with {haven}

Data come in many formats. The usual packages for importing them are:

  • {readr}: .csv and other text files (readr::read_csv())
  • {haven}: Stata (.dta), SPSS (.sav), and SAS files
  • {readxl}: Excel files

The ESS is distributed as a Stata file, so we use haven::read_dta(). In these labs we load the data directly from the web, so the .qmd file is all you need. In your own projects, you would save the file in data/ and use a relative path such as "data/ess11_lab.dta".

ess <- haven::read_dta("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seramirezruiz/seramirezruiz.github.io/master/data/ess11_lab.dta")

Labelled data 🏷

Notice that many columns are of type <dbl+lbl>: labelled doubles. {haven} keeps the value labels from Stata, so the number and its meaning travel together:

ess$gndr[1:5]
<labelled<double>[5]>: Gender
[1] 1 2 2 2 1

Labels:
 value     label
     1      Male
     2    Female
 NA(a) No answer
haven::print_labels(ess$domicil)

Labels:
 value                            label
     1                       A big city
     2 Suburbs or outskirts of big city
     3               Town or small city
     4                  Country village
     5      Farm or home in countryside
 NA(a)                          Refusal
 NA(b)                       Don't know
 NA(c)                        No answer

Refusals, “don’t know”, and “no answer” were stored as Stata extended missing values (.a, .b, .c), so {haven} already reads them as NA. Always check this in any dataset you download. Many files store them as 77, 88, or 99, and a mean computed with those values included is meaningless.

Two functions you will use often:

  • haven::as_factor(): turns a labelled variable into a factor using the labels (for categorical variables).
  • haven::zap_labels(): drops the labels and keeps the numbers (for numeric scales).
table(haven::as_factor(ess$domicil))

                      A big city Suburbs or outskirts of big city 
                            7841                             4497 
              Town or small city                  Country village 
                           11612                            14093 
     Farm or home in countryside                       Don't know 
                            2030                               39 
                         Refusal                        No answer 
                              27                               17

  AT   BE   CH   CY   DE   ES   FI   FR   GB   GR   HR   HU   IE   IS   IT   LT 
2354 1594 1384  685 2420 1844 1563 1771 1684 2757 1563 2118 2017  842 2865 1365 
  NL   NO   PL   PT   RS   SE   SI   SK

About 12% of respondents do not place themselves on the left–right scale. Is that missingness random? Probably not, and that is exactly the kind of question the measurement weeks (4 and 5) will make you ask.

Data wrangling with the {tidyverse} 🔭

The {tidyverse} is a collection of packages that share a design philosophy and a grammar, so learning one package makes it easier to learn the next. We use it because:

  • it has outstanding documentation and community support,
  • it has a consistent syntax: functions are verbs, the first argument is always the data, and the output is always a data frame, and
  • it is a convenient front-end for more advanced methods.

Base R is still powerful and stable, and in practice you will often combine both.

Tidy data 🗂

The {tidyverse} expects tidy data:

  1. Each variable forms a column.
  2. Each observation forms a row.
  3. Each type of observational unit forms a table.

The ESS is already tidy at the respondent level: one row per respondent. Point 3 matters for social scientists because we often have several levels (respondents in countries). The country-level data (e.g., democracy scores) belong in a separate table that we join when needed.

The core {dplyr} verbs

Verb What it does
dplyr::select() keep or drop columns
dplyr::filter() keep rows that satisfy a condition
dplyr::mutate() create or modify columns
dplyr::group_by() define groups in the data
dplyr::summarize() collapse groups into summary statistics
dplyr::arrange() reorder rows
dplyr::count() count observations by group

dplyr::select() 🧲

The first argument is the data frame, and then we list the columns we want:

dplyr::select(ess, cntry, agea, stfdem)

We can drop columns with -, and use helpers like starts_with() or contains():

dplyr::select(ess, -idno) # everything but idno
dplyr::select(ess, cntry, starts_with("trst")) # cntry and both trust variables

dplyr::filter() ☕

filter() keeps the rows for which a logical test is TRUE:

dplyr::filter(ess, cntry == "IT")

Combine conditions with & (and), | (or), and %in%:

dplyr::filter(ess, cntry == "IT" & agea < 30)
dplyr::filter(ess, cntry %in% c("IT", "ES", "PT", "GR"))

Activity 💡

Retrieve all respondents from Hungary ("HU") or Poland ("PL") who were not born in the country (brncntr == 2). How many are there?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
dplyr::filter(ess, cntry %in% c("HU", "PL") & brncntr == 2)

Only a few dozen people. Keep this in mind whenever you estimate anything for small subgroups in a national survey.

The pipe operator %>% 🔗

Real data work chains many steps. The pipe %>% takes the object on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right. You can read it as “and then”.

# without the pipe: nested, read from the inside out
dplyr::select(dplyr::filter(ess, cntry == "IT"), agea, stfdem)

# with the pipe: read from top to bottom
ess %>%
  dplyr::filter(cntry == "IT") %>%
  dplyr::select(agea, stfdem)

Since version 4.1.0, R also has a native pipe, |>. For everything we do in this course the two behave the same, and you will see both in the wild. I use %>%, which comes with the {tidyverse}. Keyboard shortcut: Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + M.

Activity 💡

Rewrite this step-by-step code as a single pipe:

only_italy <- dplyr::filter(ess, cntry == "IT")
only_italy_young <- dplyr::filter(only_italy, agea < 30)
final_df <- dplyr::select(only_italy_young, agea, gndr, stfdem)
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess %>%
  dplyr::filter(cntry == "IT", agea < 30) %>% # a comma inside filter() works like &
  dplyr::select(agea, gndr, stfdem)

dplyr::mutate() 👽

mutate() creates new columns (or overwrites existing ones), usually from existing variables:

ess %>%
  dplyr::mutate(age_decades = agea / 10) %>%
  dplyr::select(agea, age_decades)

Two helpers do most recoding work:

  • dplyr::if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) for binary recodes
  • dplyr::case_when() for multiple categories, evaluated top to bottom
ess %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    born_abroad = dplyr::if_else(brncntr == 2, 1, 0),
    age_group = dplyr::case_when(
      agea < 30 ~ "18-29",
      agea < 50 ~ "30-49",
      agea < 70 ~ "50-69",
      agea >= 70 ~ "70+"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(brncntr, born_abroad, agea, age_group)

Cleaning decisions are research decisions 🌿

Let’s look at the education variable:

summary(ess$eduyrs)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
    0.0    11.0    13.0    13.3    16.0    69.0     530 
ess %>%
  dplyr::filter(eduyrs > 25) %>%
  dplyr::count(eduyrs)

Some respondents report 40, 50, or even 69 years of full-time education. Are these coding errors? People who confused “years of education” with age? Actual lifelong students? You will need to make a decision: drop them, cap them (e.g., at 25), or keep them.

There is rarely a single correct answer, but there should always be a documented one. Each of these small choices is a fork in what Gelman & Loken (this week’s reading) call the garden of forking paths. Write them in your code, not in your head.

ess_clean <- ess %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    eduyrs = dplyr::if_else(eduyrs > 25, 25, eduyrs), # top-code at 25 years
    female = dplyr::if_else(gndr == 2, 1, 0),
    born_abroad = dplyr::if_else(brncntr == 2, 1, 0),
    domicil = haven::as_factor(domicil)
  ) %>%
  haven::zap_labels() # we have used the labels; drop them from the numeric scales

Activity 💡

Using ess_clean, create a variable voted equal to 1 if the respondent voted, 0 if they did not, and NA if they were not eligible (vote == 3). Then use count() to check that it worked.

Hint: case_when() returns NA for any case not covered by a condition.

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(voted = dplyr::case_when(
    vote == 1 ~ 1,
    vote == 2 ~ 0
  )) %>%
  dplyr::count(vote, voted)

Cross-tabulating the old and new variables with count() is a quick sanity check after any recode.

dplyr::group_by() and dplyr::summarize() 📊

These two usually go together. summarize() collapses a data frame into summary statistics, and group_by() makes it do so separately for each group:

ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_stfdem = mean(stfdem, na.rm = TRUE))
ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    mean_stfdem = mean(stfdem, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_stfdem = sd(stfdem, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Grouping carries over to the operations that follow. It is good practice to add .groups = "drop" (or dplyr::ungroup()) when you are done. Here is a nice explanation by Andrew Heiss of why leftover groups cause trouble.

A note on survey weights ⚖️

Unweighted ESS means describe the sample, not the population. The ESS provides anweight, which corrects for the sampling design and non-response, and for comparing or pooling countries. For descriptive statistics, use weighted.mean():

ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(
    unweighted = mean(stfdem, na.rm = TRUE),
    weighted = weighted.mean(stfdem, w = anweight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

⚠️ Order matters inside summarize(). If you write stfdem = mean(stfdem) and then weighted.mean(stfdem, anweight) in the same call, the second line uses the new one-number stfdem, and R complains that x and w have different lengths. Give summaries new names.

dplyr::arrange() and dplyr::count() 🗃

ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_stfdem = weighted.mean(stfdem, anweight, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(mean_stfdem)) # descending order

count() is a shortcut for group_by() + summarize(n = n()):

ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::count(cntry, born_abroad)

Activity 💡

Which three countries have the most positive average view of immigration (imwbcnt)? Does the ranking change if you only look at respondents born in the country? (Use weighted means.)

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(imm = weighted.mean(imwbcnt, anweight, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(imm, n = 3)
ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::filter(born_abroad == 0) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(imm = weighted.mean(imwbcnt, anweight, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(imm, n = 3)

Joining data: bringing in the country level (for you to read later) 🤝

We often want to combine individual-level survey data with country-level information. Here we use the V-Dem electoral democracy index (v2x_polyarchy, 0–1). The file contains the most recent year in our extract (2019).

vdem <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seramirezruiz/seramirezruiz.github.io/master/data/vdem_2019.csv")
vdem

The {dplyr} join family:

  • dplyr::left_join(x, y): keep all rows of x and add matching columns from y
  • dplyr::inner_join(x, y): keep only rows that match in both
  • dplyr::full_join(x, y): keep all rows of both
  • dplyr::anti_join(x, y): rows of x with no match in y (great for checking why a join failed)

Always be explicit about the key with by =:

country_df <- ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_stfdem = weighted.mean(stfdem, anweight, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::left_join(vdem, by = "cntry")

country_df

We could also join vdem directly onto the 40,000 respondents with the same code. Each respondent then gets their country’s democracy score, which is the typical setup for the multilevel models in Week 7.

Activity 💡

Using country_df, are citizens more satisfied with democracy in countries that V-Dem rates as more democratic? Compute the correlation between mean_stfdem and v2x_polyarchy with cor(). Which two countries have the lowest polyarchy scores?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
cor(country_df$mean_stfdem, country_df$v2x_polyarchy)
[1] 0.4314208
country_df %>%
  dplyr::arrange(v2x_polyarchy) %>%
  head(2)

A moderate positive correlation across 24 countries. Is it causal? Is it driven by the two outlying cases? (Try dropping Serbia and Hungary with filter() and computing it again.) We will plot it in Lab 3.

Reshaping with {tidyr} 🔄

Data can be stored wide (one column per measurement) or long (one row per measurement). The same information, two shapes. You will need both: long is what {ggplot2} and most models expect, and wide is often how data arrive (and how tables are printed).

Let’s compute country means for three trust variables. The result is wide:

trust_wide <- ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(
    politicians = mean(trstplt, na.rm = TRUE),
    parliament = mean(trstprl, na.rm = TRUE),
    people = mean(ppltrst, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

trust_wide

tidyr::pivot_longer()

tidyr::pivot_longer(
  data,
  cols,               # which columns to stack
  names_to = "name",  # new column that stores the old column names
  values_to = "value" # new column that stores the values
)
trust_long <- trust_wide %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(politicians, parliament, people),
    names_to = "trust_in",
    values_to = "mean_trust"
  )

trust_long

tidyr::pivot_wider()

The inverse:

trust_long %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = cntry,
    names_from = trust_in,
    values_from = mean_trust
  )

Activity 💡

With trust_long, find the object of trust (politicians, parliament, or people) with the highest mean in each country, and count how often each one comes first.

Hint: group_by() + dplyr::slice_max() + count().

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
trust_long %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cntry) %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(mean_trust, n = 1) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::count(trust_in)

In 20 of the 24 countries, Europeans trust each other more than their institutions, and politicians are the least trusted in every single country.

Functions, iteration, and our first simulation (for you to read later) 🎲

This course relies heavily on simulation. You will simulate a data-generating process, break an assumption, and watch what happens. For that you need to write functions and repeat them.

Writing functions 🏭

A good rule of thumb is DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself): once you have copy-pasted code twice, write a function.

function_name <- function(argument_1, argument_2) {
  # body: what the function does
  # the last line is what the function returns
}

Let’s write a function that standardizes a variable (z-scores), something you will do often before comparing coefficients:

zscale <- function(x) {
  (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

zscale(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
[1] -1.2649111 -0.6324555  0.0000000  0.6324555  1.2649111

Our own functions work inside {tidyverse} verbs:

ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(stfdem_z = zscale(stfdem)) %>%
  dplyr::select(stfdem, stfdem_z)

Activity 💡

This version of zscale() has a bug. What does it compute instead, and why?

zscale_buggy <- function(x) {
  x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}
➨ Click for Answer 🔓

Order of operations: division happens before subtraction, so the function computes \(x - \frac{\bar{x}}{s_x}\) instead of \(\frac{x - \bar{x}}{s_x}\). It returns numbers without complaining, which is exactly why this kind of bug is dangerous. Test your functions on inputs where you know the answer: zscale_buggy(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)) should give -1.26 ... 1.26, and it doesn’t.

Iteration with {purrr} ⚙️

Often we want to do the same thing many times. You may know for loops:

squares <- vector("numeric", 5) # pre-allocate the output
for (i in 1:5) {
  squares[i] <- i^2
}
squares
[1]  1  4  9 16 25

R is a functional language, so the {purrr} package wraps this pattern into functions. purrr::map(.x, .f) applies the function .f to every element of .x:

  • purrr::map() returns a list
  • purrr::map_dbl() returns a numeric vector
  • purrr::map_chr() returns a character vector
  • purrr::map_dfr() / purrr::list_rbind() return a data frame
purrr::map_dbl(1:5, \(i) i^2) # \(i) is shorthand for function(i)
[1]  1  4  9 16 25

Our first simulation: the sampling distribution 🎯

This week’s seminar starts from sampling distributions. Let’s build one.

Suppose the Italian ESS respondents were our entire population. We know the “true” population mean of satisfaction with democracy. In real research we only ever see one sample. What happens if we draw many?

italy <- ess_clean %>%
  dplyr::filter(cntry == "IT", !is.na(stfdem)) %>%
  dplyr::pull(stfdem) # pull() extracts a column as a vector

true_mean <- mean(italy)
true_mean
[1] 4.917724

One sample of 100 respondents:

one_sample <- sample(italy, size = 100)
mean(one_sample)
[1] 5.02

Let’s wrap this in a function and repeat it 1,000 times:

draw_sample_mean <- function(population, n) {
  mean(sample(population, size = n))
}

sample_means <- purrr::map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) draw_sample_mean(italy, n = 100))

head(sample_means)
[1] 4.44 4.93 4.94 5.01 5.09 5.05
mean(sample_means) # close to the true mean?
[1] 4.92147
sd(sample_means) # the standard error!
[1] 0.2183933

The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is the standard error. Compare it with the textbook formula \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\):

sd(italy) / sqrt(100)
[1] 0.2176438

A quick plot (we will learn {ggplot2} properly in Lab 3):

ggplot(data.frame(sample_means), aes(x = sample_means)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2f1a61", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "#cc0065", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Sample mean of satisfaction with democracy (n = 100)",
       y = "Count",
       title = "1,000 samples from the same population")

Reproducibility: sample() is random, so you get different numbers every time. Put set.seed(any_number) at the top of your document to make simulations reproducible. This one used set.seed(2026).

Activity 💡

How does the standard error change with sample size? Use purrr::map_dbl() to compute the standard deviation of 1,000 sample means for n = 25, n = 100, and n = 400.

What pattern do you see? What does it imply about the cost of doubling your precision?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
simulate_se <- function(population, n, reps = 1000) {
  means <- purrr::map_dbl(1:reps, \(i) draw_sample_mean(population, n))
  sd(means)
}

sample_sizes <- c(25, 100, 400)
purrr::map_dbl(sample_sizes, \(n) simulate_se(italy, n))
[1] 0.43527186 0.20559340 0.09915357

Each time we quadruple the sample size, the standard error roughly halves, since \(SE \propto 1/\sqrt{n}\). Doubling your precision costs four times the data. Keep this in mind when we talk about statistical power and the chance of finding “significant” effects in small studies.

Bonus activity 💡 (forking paths)

Simulate a study with no true effects: a random “treatment” and 20 outcomes that are pure noise, each tested with t.test(). How many “significant” results (p < 0.05) do you find? Repeat with a different seed.

Hint: t.test(outcome ~ treatment)$p.value extracts the p-value.

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
n <- 200
treatment <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)

p_values <- purrr::map_dbl(1:20, \(i) {
  outcome <- rnorm(n) # pure noise, unrelated to treatment
  t.test(outcome ~ treatment)$p.value
})

round(p_values, 3)
 [1] 0.357 0.740 0.070 0.231 0.989 0.095 0.773 0.019 0.705 0.496 0.904 0.685
[13] 0.222 0.880 0.989 0.578 0.410 0.780 0.594 0.893
sum(p_values < 0.05)
[1] 1

With 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, we expect about one false positive, and the probability of at least one is \(1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64\). Now imagine only the significant one gets written up.

Best practices (for you to read later) 📚

Reproducible documents with Quarto

In this course all assignments are submitted as Quarto documents (.qmd) that render from start to finish. This document is one. A .qmd interleaves text and code chunks, and rendering runs all code in a fresh session. If it renders, it reproduces.

  • Load packages and set seeds at the top.
  • Use relative paths (data/ess11_lab.dta).
  • End with sessionInfo() so readers know your R and package versions.
  • Never save your workspace (.RData). In RStudio: Tools > Global Options > General > Save workspace on exit: Never. Your scripts should be the only source of truth.

Naming

Use short, informative names without spaces: ess_clean, model_controls, 01-clean-data.R. The tidyverse style guide is a good default.

Getting help

  • ?function_name opens the documentation.
  • The error message is your friend: read it, then search for it.
  • R for Data Science (Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund) is free online.
  • AI assistants are very good at explaining errors and drafting code, and we will discuss them seriously in Week 10. The same rule applies as for any code you did not write: you are responsible for understanding and validating it. Run it on examples where you know the right answer.
